nature-nbs-220.title: Nature-based solutions: hiring ecosystems to do the work
nature-nbs-220.text: A strip of mangrove forest along a tropical coast does four jobs at once. It breaks the force of waves and wind, stores carbon, nurtures fish and holds the shoreline against erosion. That bundle of benefits is the idea behind nature-based solutions, or NBS. They are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges, while benefiting both people and biodiversity. The challenges are big ones: slowing climate change and adapting to it, securing water and food, and reducing disaster risk. Cities have their own versions. Roofs covered in plants or built to hold rain, and walls draped in greenery, can cool overheated city centers, capture rainwater, cut pollution and store carbon. The term came from practitioners in the late 2000s. The IUCN and the World Bank took it up to describe working with ecosystems rather than relying purely on engineering. The IUCN now treats NBS as an umbrella over {{ref:nature-nbs-112}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-216}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-218}} and {{ref:nature-nbs-224}}. The European Commission stresses that NBS are cost-effective and deliver environmental, social and economic benefits at once. The flood evidence is encouraging. A review of 386 cases found NBS as effective as conventional ways of handling floods, or more so, and 66% reported positive ecological outcomes. Politics has followed. Around 130 national climate pledges, known as {{ref:nature-clim-071}} documents, commit to NBS: 65% of signatories. Yet those pledges rarely become measurable action.

nature-nbs-218.title: Ecosystem-based adaptation: living defenses against a changing climate
nature-nbs-218.text: When a storm surge rolls toward a coast, a healthy reef, mangrove stand or marsh can take much of the blow. Using such living defenses on purpose is called ecosystem-based adaptation, or EbA. It uses biodiversity and ecosystem services to help people adapt to the harmful effects of climate change. In practice, EbA conserves, sustainably manages and restores forests, wetlands, mangroves and coral reefs. The goal is less harm from storms, shifting rainfall and temperature extremes. The examples are concrete. Restored reefs, mangroves and marshes soften storm surges. Trees grown among crops, a practice called {{ref:nature-nbs-247}}, help farms ride out drought. Well-managed forests hold slopes in place and prevent flash floods. EbA can work alone or alongside engineered works such as dykes, hybrid measures such as artificial reefs, and systems that warn people early. Supporters claim a long list of side benefits: better health, food and water security, fewer disasters, stored carbon and conserved biodiversity. The IUCN coined the term in 2008, and the {{ref:nature-gov-015}} defined it officially in 2009. It sits inside the wider family of nature-based solutions. Many countries cite EbA in their climate pledges under the {{ref:nature-clim-074}}. It is increasingly seen as a way to tackle hardship and the climate crisis together in developing countries, where people depend on natural resources.

nature-nbs-216.title: Ecological engineering: a small push that steers big natural forces
nature-nbs-216.text: In 1962 Howard Odum gave a name to a powerful trick: using a small input of human energy to steer large natural processes. He called it ecological engineering. The field combines ecology and engineering to design, build or restore, and manage ecosystems that serve both society and nature. Civil engineering focuses on built infrastructure; this field works with natural infrastructure and the bond between people and planet. Projects range from restored wetlands to greenhouses that turn wastewater into fertilizer, flowers and drinking water. They work at three scales: mesocosms of about 0.1 to hundreds of meters, ecosystems of about one to tens of km, and whole regions. Mitsch and Jorgensen set out five basic concepts. The field relies on ecosystems designing themselves, tests ecological theory, thinks in whole systems, saves non-renewable energy and supports {{ref:nature-eco-309}}. Choosing between designs should draw on {{ref:nature-eecon-059}}, guided by values that favor conservation.

nature-nbs-223.title: The case against nature-based solutions
nature-nbs-223.text: Not everyone cheers. The Indigenous Environmental Network calls nature-based solutions a tool for {{ref:nature-nbs-075}}. Turning non-forest land into plantations, it warns, can take land from smallholders and herders. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) adds that NBS cannot replace deep cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, or excuse delaying them. The dispute is plain: critics ask whether NBS are sold as a substitute for emission cuts, and whether they trample people's rights to land. Most case studies also come from the Global North. Of 257,266 papers on {{ref:nature-nbs-225}}, fewer than 2% mentioned cost, equity or Indigenous and local communities in their abstracts.

nature-nbs-222.title: Green plus grey: why hybrids beat either alone
nature-nbs-222.text: Should a city trust concrete or nature? Research suggests the best answer is often both. Hybrid green–grey infrastructure combines nature-based solutions with conventional built, or 'grey', infrastructure. Studies find NBS improve flood resilience but cannot act alone; they must be coordinated with grey works. Used together, the benefits reach beyond flood control to better social conditions, more stored carbon and stronger resilience planning. Researchers urge looking for such synergies rather than treating NBS as a rival to engineering.

nature-nbs-221.title: Three types of nature-based solution, from hands-off to built
nature-nbs-221.text: Nature-based solutions come in three broad types, sorted by how much people engineer the ecosystem. Type 1 barely intervenes: protecting mangroves against storms, or creating marine protected areas that export fish to nearby fishing grounds. Type 2 manages landscapes to be sustainable and do several jobs, as in growing trees among crops ({{ref:nature-nbs-247}}) or mixing tree species so forests resist shocks. Type 3 manages ecosystems intensively or creates new ones, such as planted roofs and walls or wetlands built from scratch. The typology carries a trade-off. The more services and stakeholder groups a solution targets, the less it can maximize any single one.

nature-nbs-219.title: Why ecosystem-based adaptation is slow to spread
nature-nbs-219.text: Case studies show ecosystem-based adaptation can work and can save money. So why is it not everywhere? First, nobody knows beyond what limits ecosystems can keep providing protection as the climate changes. Second, methods vary and nobody measures success the same way, so the economic case is hard to argue. Third, governance is awkward, because EbA spans the sectors that manage ecosystems and the different sectors that benefit from them. Finally, low incomes, pressing development needs, limited finance and cultural preferences about landscapes all slow its uptake.

nature-nbs-217.title: Five ways to put an ecosystem to work
nature-nbs-217.text: Mitsch and Jorgensen sorted ecological engineering designs into five classes by how the ecosystem is used. An ecosystem can solve a pollution problem, as wetlands that treat wastewater and planted beds that filter runoff do. It can be imitated to fix a resource problem, as with replacement wetlands and small planted hollows that soak up rain. It can be recovered after disturbance, as when old mine land or a lake is restored. It can be modified in an ecologically sound way. Or it can be used for benefit without upsetting its balance, as in growing trees among crops or raising several species together in fish farms.

nature-nbs-224.title: Ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction: buffers that also feed people
nature-nbs-224.text: Some of the best disaster defenses also put food on the table. Ecosystem-based disaster risk reduction, or Eco-DRR, uses ecosystems to prevent and reduce disasters. It keeps ecosystems working as buffers against dangerous natural events while they go on supplying communities with food and water. Its measures are often closely linked to those of ecosystem-based adaptation, or much the same. Because rivers and coasts cross borders, the {{ref:nature-clim-023}} calls for countries to cooperate on ecosystem-based approaches in shared river basins and coastlines. Research so far has focused on cities in the Global North. Coastal, dryland and watershed areas of the Global South need much more.

nature-nbs-225.title: Natural climate solutions: land managed for carbon
nature-nbs-225.text: Canada has set up a CAD$2B Natural Climate Solutions Fund, including CAD$885M for climate solutions in agriculture over 2021–31. Natural climate solutions are conservation, restoration and better land-management actions that increase carbon storage or avoid greenhouse gas emissions. In effect, they protect and enlarge nature's carbon sinks. The research on them is vast but lopsided. A global evidence map found 257,266 relevant papers across 22 pathways. Yet fewer than 2% mentioned cost, equity or Indigenous and local communities in their abstracts.

nature-nbs-209.title: Stormwater: where city rain goes
nature-nbs-209.text: In a forest, a heavy shower mostly disappears, because soil and plants absorb much of it. Stormwater is the water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and melted hail and snow. It has four possible fates. It can soak into the soil to become groundwater, pond on the surface, evaporate, or run off over the land as {{ref:nature-eco-275}}. Cities tilt the odds toward running off. Hard surfaces let less rain soak in, and drains rush the rest into waterways. The results are erosion and floods, with little water left to recharge groundwater. Unmanaged stormwater causes two main urban problems: flooding and water pollution. It is a major cause of flooding in cities. Most runoff reaches streams, rivers and other water bodies without any treatment. Phosphorus is one culprit it carries. Washed into lakes, it feeds blooms of algae and toxic cyanobacteria. Much of this chapter is about ways to make city rain behave more like forest rain.

nature-nbs-176.title: Flood management: living with water that rises
nature-nbs-176.text: The US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) estimates that every $1.00 spent on flood mitigation saves $4.00. Flood management, also called flood control, covers the methods used to reduce or prevent the harm floodwaters do. Floods come from a mix of causes. Some are natural, such as extreme weather upstream. Others are human, such as changes to water bodies and to how rain runs off the land. More hard surfaces make flooding worse, and so do wildfires that strip away vegetation. The methods fall into two families. Structural methods physically hold water back; non-structural methods do not. Wetlands are one of nature's own tools. They hold excess water and, especially on coasts, shield inland communities from storm surges. Protection is not cheap, and its cost rises with the number of people and the amount of property it covers. Yet floods are not simply enemies. Natural seasonal floods renew soil fertility, restore wetlands and support biodiversity.

nature-nbs-161.title: Green infrastructure: building with nature
nature-nbs-161.text: When people harness nature and use it as an infrastructure system, they have built green infrastructure. It is a network of natural or nature-like features, also called blue-green infrastructure, used to solve urban and climate problems by building with nature. Nature can shield communities from flooding and extreme heat. It can also improve the quality of air, soil and water. The list of jobs is long: managing stormwater, adapting to climate change, easing heat stress, supporting biodiversity, growing food, cleaning air and water, and offering recreation and shade. Examples range from city woodlands and planted roofs to artificial wetlands, rain-soaking gardens, basins that catch runoff and planted drainage channels, all met later in this course. The idea has deep roots. Its stormwater thinking began in mid-1980s proposals to reduce runoff volume and erosion and recharge aquifers. The term itself first appeared in the early 1990s, in a 1994 report on the Florida Greenways Project. There is still no widely agreed definition. People often stretch it to 'multifunctional' green infrastructure, meaning several functions share the same land.

nature-nbs-211.title: Urban flooding: when the drains give up
nature-nbs-211.text: Floods are not only for riverside towns. Urban flooding is the flooding of land or property in a built-up area when rain or coastal storm surges overwhelm drainage such as storm sewers. It can strike whether or not a community sits on a floodplain or near water. Anything that enlarges sealed, impermeable surfaces raises the risk. Climate change is expected to make storm surges, heavy rain and river overflows more frequent and severe. The toll is heavy. In 2020, floods caused an estimated 6,000 deaths and US$51.3B in damages worldwide. Where homes have basements, urban flooding is the main cause of basement and sewer backups, and chronically wet houses are linked to respiratory illness. Responses include grey and green infrastructure, better drainage, and shifting land use toward more vegetated open space.

nature-nbs-158.title: Constructed wetlands: marshes built to clean water
nature-nbs-158.text: A marsh can be built to clean dirty water. A constructed wetland is an artificial wetland made to treat sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater. It is engineered, but it relies on the natural work of plants, soil and microorganisms to give wastewater a secondary treatment. Roots, stems and leaves give microbes a surface to grow on while they break down organic matter. Physical, chemical and biological processes together strip out nitrogen, phosphorus and dissolved metals. Stormwater versions copy natural wetlands to capture runoff, cut nutrient loads and create varied wildlife habitat. Because they largely run themselves, their lifetime costs are far lower than conventional treatment plants, and building them is often cheaper too. The catch is space, so they lose out where land is expensive. Cattails and common reed are the main plants, though both can turn invasive outside their native range. Stormwater wetlands can also become 'ecological traps' for amphibians, whose larvae suffer from the pollutants collected there.

nature-nbs-174.title: Bioswales: planted ditches that clean the street
nature-nbs-174.text: In 1996, Portland installed 2330 lineal feet of bioswale at Willamette River Park. Small barriers called check dams cut the suspended solids entering the river by 50%. A bioswale is a channel, usually planted or mulched, that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution. Its sides slope gently, at less than 6%. The trick is patience. A bioswale keeps water as long as safely possible, because longer stays remove more pollutants. Plants catch the pollutants, which then enter the soil, where bacteria break them down. Bioswales suit streets and parking lots, where the first rain washes off car pollution. They also recharge groundwater, reduce flooding and erosion, and give pollinators habitat. There are four types: low grass, vegetated, low water use and wet. Neglect leads to costly repairs, so inspection at least once a year is advised.

nature-nbs-171.title: Sustainable drainage: making pipes behave like soil
nature-nbs-171.text: In urban areas covered mostly by hard surfaces, more than half of the rain becomes runoff. A sustainable drainage system, or SuDS, is a set of practices that make modern drainage work with natural water processes, as part of a wider green infrastructure strategy. SuDS aim to reduce the harm development does to the water cycle, especially runoff and water pollution. They often bypass traditional drains and return rainwater to natural water bodies as soon as possible. Typical parts include bioswales, porous paving, artificial wetlands, ponds that hold rain, planted roofs, rain-soaking gardens and downspouts cut off from the sewer. Plants and soil remove pollutants by adsorption, where they stick to surfaces, and by filtration and plant uptake. Cost favors them: planting a garden to handle drainage usually costs less than digging tunnels and laying pipes.

nature-nbs-184.title: Water-sensitive urban design: rain as a resource
nature-nbs-184.text: Conventional drainage treated city rain as a nuisance and sent it quickly to streams. Water-sensitive urban design, or WSUD, treats it as a resource. This planning and engineering approach builds the whole urban water cycle into city design: stormwater, groundwater, wastewater and supply. Its aims are to limit environmental harm and make cities more pleasant. The framework came out of Australia in the 1990s, and the term is used there and in the Middle East. It resembles {{ref:nature-nbs-197}} in the United States and sustainable drainage systems in the United Kingdom. Its principles include protecting urban creeks and wetlands, sending cleaner water out of cities and reusing as much stormwater, recycled water and greywater as possible. Common tools include planted filter beds, gravel trenches, porous paving, settling basins, constructed wetlands, swales and rainwater tanks. In Victoria, new housing developments must leave at least 20 percent of each site free of impervious surfaces. Regulatory barriers and institutions split across state and local government are its main obstacles.

nature-nbs-173.title: Bioretention: how a planted bed scrubs out metals
nature-nbs-173.text: In laboratory tests, planted soil beds removed 94% of zinc, 88% of copper, 95% of lead and more than 95% of cadmium at typical stormwater levels. Such a bed is a bioretention cell. Bioretention is the removal of pollutants and sediment from stormwater runoff by a planted soil area. A cell has two goals: lowering peak runoff and removing pollutants. A typical one has a sand bed, layers of filter media and plants on top. Stored water seeps into the soil below over several days. The name refers to the plants and bacteria in the media, which hold, absorb, break down and cycle contaminants. Four processes do the cleaning: filtration, adsorption, chemical change and biological breakdown. Nutrients matter downstream. Untreated nitrogen and phosphorus in runoff cause eutrophication, an overgrowth fed by excess nutrients, and well-designed media can sharply reduce both. The cells have limits. Their capacity for heavy metals runs out, so where metal loads are high the media must eventually be replaced. Soils with more than 25 percent clay, slopes over 20 percent or unstable ground may rule bioretention out.

nature-nbs-183.title: Rain gardens: small hollows that swallow storms
nature-nbs-183.text: In 1990, Prince George's County in Maryland replaced a conventional stormwater pond with something humbler: residential rain gardens. They proved highly cost-effective. A rain garden is a shallow planted hollow, also called a bioretention facility, that helps runoff soak back into the soil. It cuts the speed, amount and pollution of runoff from roofs, driveways, parking lots and compacted lawns. Plants and soil hold the water and filter its pollutants. Central urban areas can be 90 to 100 percent hard surfaces, against 5 to 10 percent in suburbs. A typical soil mix is 60% sand, 20% compost and 20% topsoil. Native plants are usually chosen because they tolerate local conditions, root deeply and add habitat. A study rain garden in Xi'an held most of 28 large storms over four years; only 5 made it overflow. Water ponding for more than 48 hours may signal clogging, one of the most common problems.

nature-nbs-197.title: Low-impact development: handling rain where it falls
nature-nbs-197.text: Conventional detention ponds in Prince George's County, Maryland, were not cost-effective and missed their water quality goals. So in 1990 the county tried low-impact development, or LID. This North American approach to land planning and engineering manages stormwater runoff as part of green infrastructure. It uses small engineered controls to copy a site's natural water regime, infiltrating, filtering, storing, evaporating and holding runoff near its source. Its five principles: conserve natural areas, minimize the impact on water flows, keep runoff rate and duration, scatter small controls across the site, and prevent pollution. Typical practices include rain gardens, pervious concrete, grassed swales and collecting rainwater. Research found LID rain gardens can hold up to 90% of the water after a major storm and release it over up to two weeks. Developers gain too, since dropping ponds on expensive land lets them build more homes on the same plot. In some municipalities LID is a cost-effective way to reduce combined sewer overflows, when pipes carrying both rain and sewage spill into rivers.

nature-nbs-203.title: Permeable paving: a parking lot that drinks
nature-nbs-203.text: Permeable paving is made of porous material, or of solid blocks with gaps, that lets stormwater pass through into the ground below. Materials include pervious concrete, porous asphalt, paving stones and interlocking pavers. The surface reduces runoff and traps suspended solids, filtering pollutants out of the water. Downstream, that means less flooding and bank erosion and steadier base flows in rivers. Where the soil cannot absorb water, the pavement stores it and releases it slowly between storms. Some estimates put it at about one third more expensive than conventional paving, though it can reduce the need for other stormwater facilities. It needs care. Without regular cleaning its pores clog and it behaves like ordinary impervious paving. It should not be used at pollution 'hot spots' such as fueling stations, where it could contaminate groundwater.

nature-nbs-210.title: Stormwater management: from street sweeping to sewer fees
nature-nbs-210.text: Sweeping a street is a form of water management. Stormwater management means controlling both the quantity and quality of stormwater, using engineered controls and everyday practices known as best management practices. These range from structures such as retention ponds to procedures such as street sweeping. Technical measures include controlling hazardous materials at the source, basins and filters, protecting natural waterways, and nature-based solutions working alongside pipes. Institutional measures include stormwater fees or utilities, asset management, updated regulations and community education. Conventional facilities let particles larger than 40 micron settle out and hold water back to reduce flooding downstream. But stormwater infrastructure is a costly long-term investment, and it performs worse as climate, cities and rules change. In the US, the Environmental Protection Agency regulates stormwater under the Clean Water Act. Farm runoff, though, counts as nonpoint source pollution and needs no permit.

nature-nbs-177.title: Structural flood control: walls, banks and reservoirs
nature-nbs-177.text: Some flood defenses are ancient: planting vegetation to hold water, terracing hillsides and digging floodways to divert it. Structural flood control reduces flood effects with physical works such as reservoirs, levees, dredging and diversion channels. Levees and bunds, which are raised banks, along with reservoirs and weirs, keep rivers from bursting their banks. Many dams keep reservoir levels low before the rainy or melt season, leaving room for floodwater. On coasts, sea walls, added beach sand and barrier islands hold back the water. Floodwater can even become a resource. Diverted onto land that absorbs it, the excess recharges groundwater and eases later droughts.

nature-nbs-178.title: Non-structural flood management: maps, rules and stilts
nature-nbs-178.text: Not every flood defense holds back water. Non-structural flood management reduces flood risk through zoning, mapping, modeling and planning. Zoning rules can limit how much is built on floodplains and other flood-prone land. Engaging stakeholders helps the public and officials agree on flood policy, including emergency and land-use planning. Property owners matter more and more. They can flood-proof homes by blocking doors and vents, waterproofing and sandbagging. Buildings can be designed for resilience, for example by raising homes on stilts, so a city recovers quickly after a flood. Unlike {{ref:nature-nbs-177}}, these methods work on land, people and buildings rather than on the water itself.

nature-nbs-167.title: Green versus grey: what the ledgers show
nature-nbs-167.text: Philadelphia faced a choice: a green plan costing $1.2 billion over 25 years, or a grey plan costing $6 billion. Comparing the two is the economics of green versus grey infrastructure, weighing the costs and benefits of green infrastructure against concrete pipes and tunnels. Philadelphia's plan was also expected to raise property values by $390 million over 45 years, increasing the city's property tax income. New York City's green plan was expected to cost $1.5 billion less than a comparable grey one. Green does not always win. A 2012 study of 479 US projects found 44% reduced costs while 31% increased them. The biggest savings came from less stormwater runoff and lower heating and cooling bills. Quality matters: a 2016 UK study found residents willing to pay more for green infrastructure that was visibly greener, accessible and multifunctional. In fragile states, upfront building costs ran up to 8% higher than for other projects.

nature-nbs-168.title: Green gentrification: when a new park prices people out
nature-nbs-168.text: A new park can be bad news for the people who live beside it. Green gentrification is the displacement of lower-income residents when new green spaces raise property values and attract wealthier people. Green amenities include parks, gardens, planted roofs and green, energy-efficient building materials. They make neighborhoods more liveable, and that is the problem. Rising housing costs can push low-income households out. Long-time residents can also be displaced culturally and politically. Greening can push out homeless people and others with poor access to housing, undoing some of its own benefits. The pattern shows up in real cities. Greening projects in Chicago have raised social justice concerns such as gentrification. A study of Los Angeles housing prices linked green infrastructure to 'green climate gentrification'. The benefits are often unevenly shared, usually serving wealthier, whiter neighborhoods. Sieg and colleagues coined the term in 2004, blending older ideas of gentrification and {{ref:nature-gov-168}}. The exact definition of this kind of gentrification is still debated. Planners are urged to combine environmental goals with social equity and to work with community residents.

nature-nbs-198.title: Sponge cities: China's bet on soaking up floods
nature-nbs-198.text: In 2012 a flood in Beijing killed 79 people. In 2014 China made the sponge city national policy. Proposed by landscape architect Kongjian Yu, a sponge city uses green infrastructure, not just drains, to manage urban water and floods. The name says it: green landscapes store, slow and soak up water like a sponge. Its philosophy reverses the pipes, reservoirs and walls of conventional engineering. Retain water at the source, slow its flow, clean it naturally and adapt where it collects. Hard urban surfaces can raise surface flow from 10% to 60% and cut infiltration to nearly zero. Pilots began in 16 districts in 2015 and grew to 87 cities by 2017. Guidelines aim for cities to collect and use 70 percent of rainwater, on 20 percent of urban area by 2020 and 80 percent by 2030. Studies show less runoff and cleaner water. But monitoring data are scarce, and 19 of 30 pilot cities have flooded since.

openers.nbs: Some of the most useful infrastructure on Earth was never poured from concrete. Nature-based solutions are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle problems people face, while benefiting both people and biodiversity. This part follows that idea from rain falling on a city street to the work of controlling floods and storing carbon. It meets the engineers who design with ecology, the hybrids that pair living systems with concrete, and the people who use ecosystems to adapt to climate change and reduce disasters. It also meets the critics, who warn that nature-based solutions can become greenwashing and a distraction from cutting emissions.
openers.what-nature-based-solutions-are: Can a restored ecosystem do a job usually given to engineers? Nature-based solutions say yes: they protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges while helping both people and biodiversity. Around that idea sit several close cousins, from ecological engineering to ecosystem-based adaptation, disaster risk reduction and natural climate solutions. This chapter sorts them out and shows why living and built defenses work best together. It also weighs the critics, who see greenwashing and an uneven evidence base.
openers.water-and-flood-solutions: When rain falls on a city, it has to go somewhere. Stormwater, the water from rain and melted hail and snow, can overwhelm storm sewers and flood a built-up area. This chapter follows the ways people reduce that harm, from classic flood control to green infrastructure, a network of nature-like features that builds with nature. It meets planted channels, shallow hollows that let rain soak in, porous paving and artificial wetlands that clean dirty water. It also meets the many names for one big idea, SuDS, WSUD and LID among them, which all make city drainage work with natural water processes.

reviews.what-nature-based-solutions-are: Nature-based solutions share one idea: protect, manage or restore ecosystems so they tackle human problems while helping biodiversity. Ecological engineering supplies the design craft, ecosystem-based adaptation and Eco-DRR aim it at climate harms and disasters, and natural climate solutions aim it at carbon. The typology shows a trade-off, since a solution that serves many groups cannot maximize any one of them. The best results come when living systems work alongside concrete rather than replacing it. Critics and barriers keep the picture honest: these solutions cannot replace emission cuts, and their evidence and finance remain uneven.
